newsitem.title: USA: Clinton ahead in final rush for votes in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Clinton ahead in final rush for votes in U.S.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole defied fatigue in a madcap dash to the campaign finish line on Monday as polls predicted victory for Clinton in Tuesday's election.

The Reuters daily tracking poll showed a late surge for Dole was now fading and Clinton had moved back out to a 7.3 percentage point lead -- enough for a comfortable win although perhaps not the popular-vote majority he covets.
A New York Times poll and a Gallup poll showed Clinton leading by 16 points, which could point to a landslide. Other surveys were somewhere between those two extremes.

Clinton suffered a late slump in some polls amid a barrage of partisan attacks focusing on his alleged character flaws and controversies surrounding Democratic party acceptance of questionable campaign funds from Asian business interests.

Reform Party candidate Ross Perot, who has hit hard at that issue, planned a last-minute television bombardment with 30-minute "infomercials" on several networks. But he remained mired in single digits in most polls.
In a speech in San Antonio, Texas on Monday, Perot said without elaboration that if Clinton were re-elected, Americans would get a leader who faced criminal charges.
"Our president, his wife and a number of his associates face serious criminal charges, some are already in prison," the Texas billionaire told a crowd of about 1,500

Some of Clinton's former associates in Arkansas have been convicted of fraud in connection with the tangled financial dealings known as the Whitewater affair. No charges have been filed against the president or first lady and they have repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.

The battle for control of Congress was close with many seats in the Senate and the House of Representatives balanced on a knife edge. Republicans, who seized control of both houses in 1994 for the first time in 40 years, seemed likely to keep their majority in the Senate but the House could still go either way.

Clinton began his day in New Hampshire. That is where he dubbed himself "the Comeback Kid" in 1992 after finishing a surprisingly strong second in that year's Democratic primary election despite a heavy pounding on character issues.

That incident previewed two enduring themes of the Clinton presidency -- his political tenacity and a capacity to recover from hard blows and the persistent scandals that have clung to him throughout his political career.

Later, speaking to a fired-up crowd that filled a sports arena in Cleveland, Ohio, he urged his supporters to be sure to vote. "Are you ready for tomorrow? Will you be there?" he shouted, getting an affirmative roar in response.
Clinton was looking to make history as the first Democratic president re-elected since Franklin Roosevelt in 1944. The mood aboard his plane was euphoric.

The big question was whether Clinton could win more than 50 percent of the popular vote. Having won with only 43 percent in 1992, he was anxious to win a majority, enabling him to claim a wide mandate for his second term.

Dole, on the closing day of a 96-hour non-stop marathon that has taxed his 73-year-old body to the limits, drew several thousand people in the pre-dawn cold to a diner In Phoenix where he ordered hot tea for his sore throat.
At a rally in Houston, a hoarse Dole said: "I may not keep my voice but I'll keep my word, I'll keep my word."
Flanked by former President George Bush and his wife Barbara, Dole said he was proud to be with a couple who brought integrity to the White House, "and we miss it, we miss it, we miss it."

His final 24-hour-schedule took him to Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Louisiana, Tennesee and Iowa before ending in with a symbolic rally in the late President Harry Truman's hometown of Independence, Missouri early on Tuesday. Truman scored the biggest upset victory in modern U.S. presidential election history in 1948 over Republican Thomas Dewey.
Dole planned to vote in his birthplace of Russell, Kansas, which neighbours Missouri.

From Cleveland, Clinton was to hopscotch by air across the U.S. mid-section, stopping in Lexington, Kentucky, Des Moines, Iowa and Sioux Falls, South Dakota, before flying home to Little Rock, Arkansas to vote.
